title: Google to Buy Spirit Airlines' Business Data for $10 Million to Train AI
excerpt: The bankrupt airline's internal emails, operational data, and communications will be de-identified and used for AI model training, pending bankruptcy court approval on Wednesday.
body:
• Alphabet's Google is acquiring internal business data from bankrupt Spirit Airlines for $10 million, saying it plans to use the data for product development and AI model training.
  • The data includes employee emails, Microsoft Teams messages, spreadsheets, calendars, and marketing and operations data — all to be de-identified before the sale is finalized.
  • A U.S. bankruptcy judge will consider approving the data sale at a Wednesday court hearing; a competing $7.5 million bid from AI data company Mercor was also submitted.
  • Spirit ceased operations in May 2026 after 34 years, brought down by high debt, surging fuel costs, and two Chapter 11 filings in less than two years.

Google is set to purchase the internal business data of defunct Spirit Airlines for $10 million, marking an unusual asset sale from a bankrupt carrier and an early example of a major technology company openly acquiring enterprise data to train AI models.

Alphabet's Google submitted the winning bid for a trove of Spirit Airlines' operational data, according to Reuters. The acquisition covers employee emails, Microsoft Teams messages, spreadsheets, calendars, and marketing, productivity, and operations data accumulated over the airline's 34-year history.

What Google Is Buying

The data set is notable for its breadth. It spans the full range of internal communications and workflows that kept a major U.S. airline running — the kind of real-world enterprise data that AI companies have struggled to access at scale.

Google said it plans to use the data for product development and to train its AI models. The company specified that all data will be de-identified before the sale is completed, meaning it will contain no customer information or personally identifiable information.

Spirit also received a $7.5 million bid from Mercor, an AI data company, underscoring the growing market for enterprise datasets as AI firms seek training material beyond the publicly available text and images that powered earlier model generations.

Bankruptcy Court Approval Pending

A U.S. bankruptcy judge is scheduled to consider approving the data sale at a hearing on Wednesday. The transaction is part of Spirit's broader asset disposition process as the airline liquidates everything from aircraft and engines to airport gates and route authorities to repay creditors.

Spirit Airlines shut down operations on May 2, 2026, ending a turbulent period that included two Chapter 11 bankruptcy filings in less than two years — the first in November 2024 and the second in August 2025. A last-minute plan for roughly $500 million in federal support fell through, and soaring fuel costs tied to geopolitical tensions pushed the airline past the point of recovery.

A New Frontier for AI Training Data

The deal highlights a shift in how AI companies are sourcing training data. As the supply of publicly available text, images, and code has been largely exhausted, firms like Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic have turned to licensed and proprietary datasets. Bankruptcy estates represent a new source — companies that no longer exist but whose operational data retains value for training AI systems to understand enterprise workflows.

For Google, the Spirit data could help improve Gemini's ability to handle complex enterprise tasks such as scheduling, internal communications, project management, and operational analytics — capabilities central to its push to sell AI tools to businesses through Google Cloud.

Privacy and Precedent

The sale raises questions about the emerging market for bankrupt companies' data assets. While Google has committed to de-identification, the transaction could set a precedent for how corporate data is valued and sold in bankruptcy proceedings, potentially making enterprise datasets a standard line item alongside physical assets and intellectual property.

The bankruptcy court's decision on Wednesday will be closely watched by AI companies and privacy advocates alike, as it could establish a framework for similar transactions in future corporate liquidations.
